title: Slate & Scallion menu refresh: neutralize six mixed-lighting dish shots to a shared grey-card target, author the dark/amber house grade, and triage the two brand marks for print
grounding_note: Adapted from a real Upwork restaurant-menu-refresh brief; the real client brand is laundered to the fictional 'Slate & Scallion — Ramen & Sushi House' and used consistently in every field (brief, inputs, outputs, workflow, logo, SVG). The original brief asked for a refreshed tri-fold dine-in menu (dark background, hero food photography, red accent, ramen/sushi aesthetic) adding new ramen bowls and a Wagyu section. The page typesetting itself is layout COMPOSITION, which is NOT an available Adobe-connector capability (document_render_vector only EXPORTS an already-authored .ai), so this engagement is deliberately scoped to the genuinely connector-doable and genuinely HARD production work that feeds the layout: (1) taking a set of newly-shot dish photographs that were captured across several sessions under DIFFERENT lighting — each a full-resolution DSLR frame with a physical 18% grey reference card placed in frame — and driving all of them to ONE cohesive brand look, correcting each frame to the grey card first and then authoring the same dark/amber split-tone grade on top so the set reads as matched; (2) preparing two placement-ready cut-outs for the crowded ramen section; (3) delivering print-exact crops at 300 DPI, reachable by DOWNSCALE ONLY from the camera-scale captures; (4) handling the TWO brand marks correctly — one is a flat rasterized logo that must become clean vector, the other is a photographed painted brush mark that must NOT be vectorized; (5) building a premium dark background texture; and (6) exporting a proof of the client's existing authored .ai. The distinctive quality of the deliverable — the neutralized, cohesive, dark/amber house look landed to a measurable target across six mixed-lighting frames — is the agent's decision, not a preset and not the client's template. No layout is composed by the connector.
one_line_ask: Take six dish photos shot under mismatched lighting (each a full-res DSLR frame with a grey card in frame), neutralize every frame to that card and author one cohesive dark/amber house grade across the whole set, then prep the cut-outs, print crops, the two brand marks (vectorize the flat logo, isolate the photographed brush mark), the dark background texture, and a proof export — all matched and placement-ready for Slate & Scallion's menu refresh.
full_brief: Slate & Scallion is a ramen and sushi house refreshing its dark, photography-led dine-in menu; they are adding new ramen bowls and a Wagyu section. Their designer hand-typesets the page in an existing Illustrator source, so this job is the PHOTOGRAPHY and BRAND-ASSET production that has to be handed over drop-in ready. The problem: the new dishes were shot over several evenings by different people on our full-frame camera, so the raws do NOT match — some were lit by cool window light, some under warm tungsten, one was shot on-flash and reads bright and blue, one has a green cast off the kitchen fluorescents, and one hero was shot slightly off-level. On the menu these will sit side by side, so a mismatched set looks amateur. To make matching checkable, every shot was taken with a small 18% neutral grey reference card laid at the edge of the table. We need the whole set to look like it came from one shoot: use the grey card in each frame as your neutral truth, correct each frame's white balance and exposure to it individually by eye (they will each need a DIFFERENT correction — do not assume one setting fits all), and only then apply the brand look uniformly. The brand look is fixed and it is the point of the job: a moody dark table, deep near-black shadows, broth and garnish highlights that still glow warm, and the red chili-oil / red brand accents reading rich against the dark — an amber-warm, low-key grade, not a flat filter. When you are done, the grey card must look neutral in every frame and the darkest part of the dark table must sit at the same deep point across all six; hand back the per-frame corrections you dialed (temperature / tint / exposure) and the shared look settings so we can verify the set is actually matched and not just eyeballed. Then: for the crowded ramen section the designer needs two bowls knocked out to clean transparency so they can tuck against type without a hard photo edge; the tonkotsu bowl also needs a tall menu-cell crop at exactly 900x1350 px (3x4.5 in at 300 DPI) and the Wagyu hero needs a wide banner crop at exactly 2100x750 px (7x2.5 in at 300 DPI) — both must come straight out of the camera-scale files with no enlargement. We are also handing you our two brand marks and they are NOT the same kind of file: one is our logo delivered only as a flat rasterized PNG on a white background — we need that as a crisp print-ready vector — and the other is a PHOTOGRAPH of the hand-painted brush mark that hangs in the dining room, which we want isolated to transparency as a header graphic; treat each the right way. Finally, prep a premium dark background texture from a licensed dark-slate stock so the menu ground reads tactile and not a flat fill, and give us a proof export of the current authored .ai so the team can see where these assets will land. Deliverables: the six matched, brand-graded dish photos, two transparent ramen cut-outs, the two print-exact crops, the vectorized logo, the isolated brush-mark header, the dark background texture, and the menu proof.

inputs.name: tonkotsu_ramen_coolwindow_raw.jpg

Full-resolution DSLR capture, long edge approximately 4000 px (a real camera file, not a small web-size render).
inputs.realism_notes: Session A, cool window light: the grey card should visibly read slightly blue, so the correct fix is to WARM this frame. Carries red chili oil so it also exercises the red-accent hue push. Grey card in frame is the neutral truth the agent grades toward by eye. Declared at camera scale (~4000x2667, 3:2 DSLR) so the tonkotsu-derived 900x1350 print cell is reached by DOWNSCALE only; output px never exceed source px.

inputs.realism_notes: Session B, flat/low-contrast, near-neutral WB: this frame mostly needs contrast/black-point and the shared look rather than a big WB move. Second bowl for the transparent cut-out. No dominant red accent. Camera scale ~4000x2667.

Red/warm marbling gives the hue-band accent real subject matter. This is the frame cropped to the wide 2100x750 banner. inputs.name: salmon_nigiri_flatlay_flash_raw.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal flat-lay food photograph of five pieces of salmon nigiri on a dark slate board, glossy orange-pink salmon over pressed rice, a smear of wasabi, on-camera FLASH giving a bright, slightly blue-cool and slightly overexposed look with hard specular highlights, a small flat 18% neutral grey reference card on the slate at the lower-right edge clearly visible, real rice grain and fish sheen, documentary realism, no text, no logo. Full-resolution DSLR capture, long edge approximately 4000 px.
inputs.realism_notes: Session D, on-flash: bright, cool and a touch overexposed, so the correct fix is to WARM and pull exposure/highlights DOWN to match the set. Salmon is orange-pink and must NOT be pushed like the red brand accent, so it tests restraint in the hue-band step. Camera scale ~4000x2667.

inputs.name: chirashi_bowl_fluoro_raw.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal overhead food photograph of a chirashi sushi bowl on a dark slate table, assorted sashimi and tamago over sushi rice, ikura, shiso, under kitchen FLUORESCENT lighting that gives the whole frame a noticeable green-cyan cast, a small flat 18% neutral grey reference card on the slate at the lower-right edge clearly visible where the green cast is obvious on the grey, documentary realism, no text, no logo. Full-resolution DSLR capture, long edge approximately 4000 px.
inputs.realism_notes: Session E, fluorescent green cast: this frame needs a magenta TINT correction (green->magenta axis), not just a temperature move, so it forces the agent to use both axes of white balance rather than only warm/cool. Camera scale ~4000x2667.

inputs.name: slate_scallion_logo_flat_whitebg.png
inputs.gen_prompt: Flat 2D restaurant logo for 'Slate & Scallion' on a solid WHITE background (not transparent): a stylized red brushstroke ramen bowl with a rising scallion/steam mark, the wordmark 'Slate & Scallion' in a clean modern serif beneath it, single red accent color #C0392B plus near-black, crisp flat vector-style edges, no photographic texture, generous white margin around the mark, centered, high contrast. High-resolution flat export, long edge approximately 3000 px.
inputs.realism_notes: Delivered as a flat raster PNG on a WHITE ground (the client only has a rasterized export), at a high-res ~3000 px long edge so the trace has clean edges to follow. White background + margin is deliberate: the correct prep is knock the white to transparency and crop to bounds BEFORE tracing, or the vector trace boxes in the white rectangle. This is the mark that SHOULD be vectorized.

inputs.name: brushmark_sign_photo_raw.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal photograph of a single hand-painted black-red brush-stroke mark on a hanging dark indigo noren fabric curtain in a dim restaurant, real brush texture with visible bristle streaks and ink bleed, soft directional light, faint fabric weave and gentle folds, the painted mark clearly the main subject against the plain indigo cloth, no text, no logo, documentary realism. Full-resolution DSLR capture, long edge approximately 4000 px.
inputs.realism_notes: This is a PHOTOGRAPH of the physical painted brush mark, with real lighting, brush texture and fabric, shot on the same camera (~4000 px long edge). The correct treatment is to knock the plain indigo background to transparency with remove_background (the painted mark is the clear main subject); VECTORIZING this would return a flat black silhouette and destroy the brush texture. It is the triage twin of the flat logo and getting it wrong is invisible until inspected.

inputs.name: slate_scallion_menu_existing.ai
inputs.gen_prompt: Represents the client's EXISTING authored Adobe Illustrator tri-fold menu source (six panels, dark near-black ground, red accent rules and section headers, placeholder image frames, section labels 'Small Plates / Sushi Bowls / Artisan Ramen / Donburi / Rolls / Nigiri-Sashimi'). This is a genuine authored .ai supplied by the client; the connector only EXPORTS it via document_render_vector, it does not compose it.
inputs.realism_notes: Authored input asset, NOT connector-generated layout. It exists so document_render_vector has a real .ai to export to a print-ready proof. In a real run the client uploads their actual .ai.

inputs.name: dark_slate_texture_stock.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal seamless dark slate stone surface texture, charcoal grey-black, subtle natural mineral veining and matte sheen, very even lighting, premium restaurant menu background plate, high resolution, no objects, no text, slight natural surface grain.
inputs.realism_notes: Stands in for a licensed Adobe Stock texture (the workflow licenses it via asset_license_and_download_stock before editing). Dark but not pure black so darken-light-portions + grain produce a visible premium result rather than mud.

outputs.name: cohesive_graded_set_x6.png
outputs.spec: The six dish photos delivered as ONE matched set: each corrected by eye to its in-frame grey card until the card looks neutral, the darkest slate corner landed at a common deep near-black across all six, then the same authored dark/amber low-key house grade applied uniformly (deep shadows, warm-glowing broth/garnish highlights, red accents lifted). Agent MUST report the per-frame white-balance (temperature + tint) and exposure corrections it dialed AND the shared look settings, so 'matched' is verifiable from the applied-settings log, not asserted. Full-res PNG each. Acceptance (grader-checked): grey card neutral (R~=G~=B within tolerance) in every frame; darkest slate corner at a common near-black across all six, deep but not clipped to zero; reported per-frame corrections non-identical across the warm vs cool frames.

connector_workflow.inputs_from: tonkotsu_ramen_coolwindow_raw.jpg, shoyu_ramen_flat_raw.jpg, spicy_miso_ramen_tungsten_raw.jpg, wagyu_donburi_hero_offlevel_raw.jpg, salmon_nigiri_flatlay_flash_raw.jpg, chirashi_bowl_fluoro_raw.jpg, slate_scallion_logo_flat_whitebg.png, brushmark_sign_photo_raw.jpg, slate_scallion_menu_existing.ai
connector_workflow.note: Upload the six mixed-lighting dish raws (each a full-res DSLR frame with its in-frame grey card), the flat white-bg logo PNG, the photographed brush-mark, and the client's authored .ai into the working project so the grade and prep chains run against real references. Single ingest; not counted as difficulty.
The Wagyu hero was shot ~4deg off-level; level the horizon BEFORE any tonal work so the later banner crop is not fighting a tilt.

Frame 1 (cool window light): WARM the temperature by eye until the in-frame grey card looks neutral, then set the shared dark/amber house look — deepen blacks to the common near-black point, hold broth/egg highlights, lift shadow warmth. This frame's correction direction is warm; it will differ from every other frame. Report the per-frame WB (temp/tint) + exposure dialed here.

Frame 2 (flat, near-neutral WB): the card is already close to neutral so the WB move is small; the real work here is contrast + landing the SAME deep near-black point and the SAME amber house look as frame 1 so the two ramen bowls read identical when placed side by side.

Frame 3 (warm tungsten): the grey card reads strongly ORANGE, so the correct WB move is to COOL the temperature toward neutral BEFORE the shared amber look is applied. Applying the same warm-up used on frame 1 here would push this frame orange and break the set — the correction must be derived per frame from this card, not copied.
Frame 4 (straightened Wagyu hero, mild warm ambient): pull the card to neutral (slight cool), then the shared house look at the same black point. Consumes the straightened Wagyu, not the raw.

Frame 5 (on-flash, bright + cool): WARM toward the neutral card AND pull exposure/highlights DOWN so its brightness matches the low-key set, then the shared look. Bright-and-cool needs the opposite exposure direction from the darker frames.

Frame 6 (fluorescent green cast): neutralizing this card needs the TINT axis (green->magenta), not just temperature; correct on both WB axes to the card, then the shared house look. Using only warm/cool here leaves a visible green cast the card would expose.

Authored accent on the tonkotsu: on the red hue band only, lift saturation/luminance so the red chili oil and red brand accent read rich against the dark plate, WITHOUT dragging the amber broth toward orange (that lives in a different hue band). Per-hue reasoning, not a global vibrance push.

Same red-hue-band accent on the spicy-miso chili oil so its red matches the tonkotsu's red exactly; the shared accent target must be consistent across the ramen frames or the reds read as two different colors on the page.

On the Wagyu, lift the red/orange marbling hue band so the seared beef reads rich; restrained relative to the chili-oil push (marbling is orange-red, not pure chili red) so it does not go artificial. Frame 5 salmon is deliberately NOT pushed — its orange-pink is not the brand red.

Knock the graded tonkotsu bowl to full transparency (alpha PNG) so it can sit tight to type in the crowded ramen section without a hard photo edge. remove_background auto-detects the bowl subject; no select->invert->fill.
Second knock-out: the graded shoyu bowl to transparency for the same crowded section, so two bowls can overlap type cleanly.

Reframe the tonkotsu cut-out to the tall menu cell at EXACTLY 900x1350 px (3.0x4.5 in @300 DPI). The cut-out inherits the ~4000x2667 camera-scale resolution of the tonkotsu source, so 900x1350 is DOWNSCALE/reframe only (output px <= source px), alpha preserved; onSubjectClipping='extract' (never 'expand') so no generative canvas extension can occur and the frame is never enlarged past source pixels.

Reframe the finished Wagyu hero to the wide banner at EXACTLY 2100x750 px (7.0x2.5 in @300 DPI). The Wagyu frame is ~4000x2667 camera scale, so 2100x750 is DOWNSCALE/reframe only (output px <= source px); onSubjectClipping='extract' so no generative expansion; never enlarged past source pixels.

PREP step 1 of the flat logo before tracing: knock the solid WHITE ground to transparency. Skipping this and tracing the raw white-bg PNG would box the white rectangle into the vector — the classic un-prepped-trace failure.
PREP step 2: crop tight to the now-transparent mark's bounds so the trace is not padded with empty margin. Prep-before-trace discipline (knock-to-transparency -> crop-to-bounds) precedes vectorize.
Trace the PREPPED flat logo to a clean SVG (red #C0392B + near-black), no boxed white ground. This is the correct treatment for the FLAT rasterized mark.

TRIAGE TWIN of the flat logo: the second mark is a PHOTOGRAPH, so it must NOT be vectorized (that returns a flat black silhouette and kills the brush texture). remove_background auto-detects the painted brush-stroke as the main subject against the plain indigo noren and knocks the fabric to transparency, PRESERVING the real brush texture and ink bleed as a raster header graphic. The correct treatment for the PHOTOGRAPHED mark — the opposite of the flat logo's prep-then-vectorize path. Choosing vectorize here is the invisible-until-inspected failure.
Search + license + download a dark-slate stock texture (license BEFORE editing). Stands in for dark_slate_texture_stock; the one legitimate new asset load in the workflow.
Darken the texture's light portions so it reads as a premium dark menu ground rather than a flat mid-grey, matching the dark tables in the graded photos.
Add fine grain so the darkened slate has tactile premium texture = menu_background_texture. This is a standalone texture asset, not an opaque plate over a photo.

Export the client's EXISTING authored Illustrator menu .ai to a print-ready PNG proof. render_vector only EXPORTS the authored source; it composes nothing — the page typesetting stays the designer's hand work, correctly out of connector scope.

chaining_note: Every step after the single ingest (1) consumes a prior named output or a named raw within uploaded_assets. The grade trunk is ADAPTIVE, not repeated: step 2 straightens the Wagyu; steps 3-8 grade the six frames with SIX DIFFERENT corrections (warm / small / cool / slight-cool / warm+darken / green-tint) each driven by eye to its own in-frame grey card, then all landed on one shared dark/amber look and common black point. Steps 9-11 add the red-hue-band accent to the three frames that carry red (tonkotsu, miso, wagyu marbling) at a shared red target, deliberately sparing the salmon. Steps 12-13 knock two graded bowls to transparency; 14 crops the tonkotsu cut-out to the exact ramen cell (900x1350) downscale-only from the ~4000x2667 source, 15 crops the Wagyu accent to the exact banner (2100x750) downscale-only. The two-mark triage runs in parallel: 16-17-18 PREP-then-vectorize the flat logo (knock white -> crop to bounds -> trace), while 19 knocks the PHOTOGRAPHED brush mark to transparency via remove_background (never traced) — the opposite correct treatment. 20-21-22 license a stock slate texture and build the dark grain background. 23 exports the authored .ai proof. No step starts from a free-floating asset except the legitimate stock license at 20.
difficulty_rationale: Depth, not breadth: 23 calls / 12 distinct tools, but the difficulty is in adaptive reasoning across dependent steps, not step count. The hard core is a cross-asset consistency problem — six frames shot under five different lighting conditions, each carrying an in-frame grey card, that must be individually corrected by eye (each a DIFFERENT white-balance direction, one needing the tint axis, one needing exposure pulled down) and only then unified under one authored dark/amber house grade to a common black point, with the agent required to REPORT the per-frame settings it dialed so 'matched' is checkable by the grader. Layered on top: an authored red-hue-band accent held consistent across three frames while sparing a fourth; a triage between two superficially-parallel brand marks that need OPPOSITE correct treatments (vectorize the flat logo vs remove-background the photographed mark); prep-before-trace discipline (knock-to-transparency + crop-to-bounds before vectorize); and two print-exact 300-DPI crops reachable by downscale only from the camera-scale captures. The page typesetting is correctly excluded as out-of-connector-scope (document_render_vector EXPORTS only), which is itself the feasibility judgment the task tests. All steps are [C] headless, fully autonomous, gen-free.
hardness_rationale: FAILURE GATE the agent can trip via a wrong DECISION, not a self-measurement: the six frames each carry an 18% grey reference card, and the agent must neutralize each BY EYE toward that card and land the darkest slate corner at a common near-black, then hand back the per-frame WB (temperature+tint)+exposure it dialed and the shared look settings. A wrong craft decision is visible — a card still showing a cast, or an applied-settings log revealing one global warm-up copied across frames (which shoves the tungsten miso frame orange while barely touching the cool frames) — so the naive 'the brand look is warm, warm everything' path fails the match. HUMAN-HARD ELEMENTS: (1) cross-asset white-balance/tone consistency to an in-frame grey-card target across six differently-lit frames, each needing a distinct correction including one green->magenta tint move and one exposure-down move — far harder than a single hero; (2) triage of two look-alike brand marks needing opposite correct treatments (flat logo -> prep+vectorize vs photographed brush mark -> remove_background), where a wrong choice is invisible until inspected; (3) an authored dark/amber split-tone look plus a red-hue-band accent reasoned from image_apply_adjustments + image_adjust_hsl primitives (no preset, no auto_tone), held consistent across frames while sparing the salmon's orange-pink; (4) prep-before-trace discipline. THE TRAP: the naive path applies one global warm-up to the whole set because 'the brand look is warm' — which shoves the already-warm tungsten miso frame orange and barely touches the cool frames, so the set fails to match; a second trap is vectorizing the photographed brush mark (returns a flat black silhouette); a third is tracing the raw white-background logo (boxes the white rectangle into the SVG). MEASURABLE ACCEPTANCE (grader-checked, the agent never reads these values): grey card neutral (R~=G~=B within tolerance) in all six frames; a common near-black point deep but not clipped to zero; the reported per-frame and shared parameters non-identical across warm vs cool frames; crops at exactly 900x1350 and 2100x750 px @300 DPI, each reached by downscale from the ~4000x2667 sources (output px <= source px); and a clean logo SVG with no boxed ground.
